headline: High: dexter’s autonomous broad egress and API use can leak or misapply dbt-generated outputs, while shared file/workspace assumptions create injection and conflict risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: dbt-core can emit artifacts and read/write warehouse-facing outputs, while dexter uses autonomous execution and a scratchpad file surface. If dexter ingests dbt-produced files or logs as instructions, prompt injection is plausible in default workflows. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF dexter reads dbt-generated files or logs as instruction-bearing text
IF a shared workspace or scratchpad is used to pass content between the agents
mitigations: Separate dbt outputs from dexter scratchpad directories
Prefix all inter-agent files with machine-readable schemas
Disable autonomous parsing of free-form dbt logs
Add a manual review step before dexter consumes dbt artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: dbt-core touches data warehouse data and has allowlisted egress, while dexter touches financial and market data and can call multiple external APIs with broad egress. If either agent writes shared outputs or logs into the other’s workspace, sensitive data can flow outward. The profiles do not prove a shared filesystem, so this is inferred but credible.
conditions: IF dbt artifacts containing warehouse data are placed in dexter-accessible files
IF dexter forwards its context or scratchpad contents to external APIs
mitigations: Keep separate OS users and directories for each agent
Redact warehouse and financial fields before handoff
Restrict dexter API calls to non-sensitive prompts
Audit outbound requests for embedded file contents

C_capability_conflict.rationale: dbt-core can interact with a data warehouse, and dexter can run autonomously with multiple instances and broad API access. Overlapping writes to shared mutable resources are plausible if both target the same warehouse tables or shared files, but the profiles do not show direct filesystem write overlap. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same warehouse tables or shared output directory
IF no external locking or transaction coordination is configured
mitigations: Assign disjoint schemas or table prefixes
Enable locking or transactional guards on shared resources
Run only one writer per resource at a time
Use separate scratchpad directories per instance

D_cascading_error.rationale: dexter’s autonomous execution and broad API access make it likely to act on upstream outputs, while dbt-core can generate warehouse-facing transformations that dexter may treat as authoritative. If dexter consumes dbt results without verification, bad transformations can cascade into external actions or reports. The default autonomy raises this to high.
conditions: IF dexter uses dbt outputs as factual inputs without validation
IF dexter triggers downstream API calls or reports from those outputs
mitigations: Require checksum or schema validation on dbt outputs
Insert a human approval gate before dexter acts
Limit dexter to read-only analysis of dbt artifacts
Log source provenance for every downstream action

E_compliance.rationale: dbt-core touches data warehouse data, while dexter touches financial and market data and sends requests to third-party APIs such as OpenAI, Exa, Tavily, and LangSmith. If regulated financial or warehouse data enters dexter’s external calls, residency and retention obligations can be breached. The pairwise compliance risk is driven mainly by dexter’s documented external API surface.
conditions: IF warehouse or financial data is included in prompts sent to dexter APIs
IF retention or residency rules apply to the shared data class
mitigations: Block regulated data from dexter prompts
Configure data-minimization filters before API calls
Review vendor DPAs and retention settings
Use synthetic or masked datasets for dexter runs
